content.text: Video Quiz Course Video Only Sheila Morrissey Amanda Robb Understand what is a base in chemistry. Learn about the properties of bases and various types of bases. Explore examples about each type of base and gain practical insights. In chemistry, a base is defined as a molecule in an aqueous solution that can accept protons or donate electrons. They often taste bitter and are slippery to the touch. They are classified using the pH scale, a scale that measures the extent to which a solution is acidic, basic, or neutral. Bases fall on the high end of the scale, above 7, with weak bases (i.e. baking soda) being around 7-10 and strong bases (i.e. bleach) being around 10-14. Bases typically contain an OH- ion, meaning an oxygen atom bonded to one hydrogen atom. Acids, on the other hand, contain an H+ ion. Together, acids and bases react and form water. Create your account Video Quiz Course Video Only A base in chemistry has several distinct properties that separate it from acids and solutions with a neutral pH. The following list includes a few examples: Reaction with Acids: When mixed with acids, bases undergo a chemical reaction. The OH- and H+ groups combine, and the leftover atoms form a variety of products including carbon dioxide and various salts. Bitter Taste: Because they contain an OH- ion, bases usually taste bitter. Acids, of course, taste acidic. pH Value: By definition, all bases have a pH greater than 7. The acronym pH stands for "potential hydrogen" and is a logarithmic scale that measures the acidity of a solution. Turn pH Indicators Blue: A pH indicator is designed to have a specific reaction with acids and bases and will typically turn color according to the strength of the acid or base. By gauging this color-change, one can estimate the strength of a base or an acid. Bases typically turn the indicator various shades of green or blue. Slippery to Touch: Strong bases react with the oils in our skin, and the product of the reaction is similar to soap. This explains why bases feel slippery to the touch.Examples of BasesBelow is a list of base examples found in everyday life along with their formulas and their common uses. Baking Soda: Baking soda, also known as sodium bicarbonate, is a base with the formula NaHCO3. It has a pH around 8.3 and is used for everything from odor absorption to teeth whitening. Sodium bicarbonate, also known as baking soda. Soap: Although there are many types with various formulas, soaps are bases and typically have a pH around 10. One example is C17 H35 COONa. Soaps have a unique property where they are non-polar and polar at opposite ends of the molecule. As such, they are able to bond with both water and oils and can suspend the oils in a solution that can then be carried down the drain. Bleach: Bleach is a powerful base also known as sodium hypochlorite. Its formula is NaOCl, and it has a pH around 12. Bleach has been used as both a sterilizing agent and a stain remover for centuries. Tums: Tums is a brand name for calcium carbonate antacid tablets. Calcium carbonate has the formula CaCO3 and has a pH of about 11. The tablets are intended to treat "heart burn" or "acid reflux" which are both caused by excessive acid buildup in the stomach. Taking Tums will neutralize some of the stomach acid, reducing the amount of H+ ions and bringing the acid levels back down to normal. Antacid tablets like Tums are used to neutralize excess acid in the stomach. Lime: Lime or "slaked lime" is the common name for the chemical calcium hydroxide. Calcium hydroxide has the formula Ca(OH) 2 and has a pH of about 12.5. The chemical is often used on lawns to neutralize acids in the soil and raise the pH, which can promote a healthier growing environment for many grass species. Bases are frequently used in chemistry for chemical reactions. Examples of bases in chemical reactions include sodium hydroxide, NaOH, potassium hydroxide, KOH, and ammonia, NH3. Create your account Bases are typically classified into five categories depending on their composition and behavior: strong bases, weak bases, superbases, neutral bases, and solid bases. Definitions of these base categories are included below.Strong BaseA strong base is defined as a compound that fully dissociates its ions when mixed with water. Strong bases typically react violently with acids and have a pH between 10 and 14. Two examples are sodium hypochlorite and potassium hydroxide. Strong bases make for good disinfectants and powerful cleaners.Weak BaseA weak base is defined as a compound that does not fully dissociate its ions when mixed with water. Weak bases have a pH between 7 and 10. Two examples are baking soda and ammonia. Weak bases are useful neutralizers of acidic solutions. To unlock this lesson you must be a Study.com Member. Create your account A base in chemistry is defined as a molecule in an aqueous solution that can accept protons or donate electrons. Bases are usually bitter to taste, slippery to touch, and have a pH greater than 7 on the pH scale. Bases are the opposite of acids, and they usually contain an OH- ion, meaning an oxygen atom bonded to one hydrogen atom. Examples of bases that people might encounter in everyday life include baking soda (sodium bicarbonate), soaps, bleach (sodium hypochlorite), Tums (calcium carbonate), and lime (calcium hydroxide). Bases are often classified into five types: strong bases, weak bases, superbases, neutral bases, and solid bases. The first three types simply vary in their reactivity. The last two types are unique in their behavior and composition and are much less common. To unlock this lesson you must be a Study.com Member. Create your account What is a Base?As seen on the pH scale, bases describe solutions with a pH greater than seven, and there is a range of how basic a solution can be. A base is the opposite of an acid. The 'H' in 'pH' stands for hydrogen. The origin of the 'p' in 'pH' is somewhat debatable, but we can think of pH as the power of hydrogen or the potential of hydrogen. pH is defined as -log(H+), or the -log of the activity of hydrogen. Bases differ from acids in their potential for accepting rather than releasing hydrogen ions. The more free hydrogen a solution has, the more acidic it is and the lower its pH value. Solutions with a high pH value, such as drain cleaner, are very basic and thus have a high potential for accepting hydrogen ions. Properties and Examples of BasesBases tend to taste bitter and feel slippery. At home, we use bases as cleaning agents and as antacid medications. Common examples of bases found at home include soaps; lye, which is found in oven cleaners, for example; milk of magnesia; and Tums. Each has a pH value greater than seven, has the potential for accepting free hydrogen, and can neutralize acids. Bases in ActionBecause bases are the opposite of acids, with acids releasing free hydrogen ions in aqueous solution and bases having the potential to accept those hydrogen ions, bases can be used to neutralize acids. The calcium carbonate found in Tums works to neutralize stomach acid by dissolving into aqueous calcium and carbonate ions. Acidity-causing, positively-charged free hydrogen ions attach to the ions, forming bicarbonate. The concentration of positively-charged free hydrogen ions is reduced, thereby reducing the acidity and raising the pH level in your stomach. A similar acid-neutralizing series of reactions is happening on a much larger scale in our oceans. As air comes into contact with the surface of the ocean, gases in the air get dissolved into the ocean water. One of these gases, carbon dioxide, is a naturally-occurring component of air that also has a continually increasing, human-caused component. The increasing carbon dioxide in the air is putting pressure on the ocean's ability to neutralize acid. As carbon dioxide dissolves into the ocean, it reacts with water to form carbonic acid. This drives a hydrogen ion to dissociate, forming bicarbonate, which can further dissociate a hydrogen ion to form carbonate. Ideally, adequate carbonate will be available for the formation of calcium carbonate by marine organisms. It's the same substance found in Tums, and it's what makes up the shells of much of Earth's marine life. We learned from our use of calcium carbonate as an antacid medication that it will dissolve to form calcium and carbonate, and the carbonate ions join hydrogen ions to neutralize the acid. This same process happens in the ocean. With increased pressure of carbon dioxide on the ocean, more hydrogen ions are formed, and the pH of the ocean decreases. Currently, the ocean has a pH level approximately 0.1 pH units lower than the pre-industrial pH. The increased acid brings increased acid neutralization by the basic calcium carbonate found in the ocean but decreases the carbonate availability and causes calcium carbonate shells to dissolve. Lesson SummaryBases are substances that, when dissolved in water, have a pH level greater than seven, taste bitter, and feel slippery. They react with acids by accepting H+ ions, giving bases the ability to neutralize acids. Bases are commonly found in cleaning products and antacid medications. In nature, an important example of a base neutralizing acid occurs in the ocean.
